query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying an ultra-thin, PVD-deposited Al2O3 layer on boride-based components will significantly improve their resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion by impeding the diffusion of aluminum into the boride substrate.
generation.material_initial_state: Boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment that are directly exposed to molten aluminum at 700–750°C, which leads to interfacial degradation as aluminum diffuses into the boride layer.
generation.intervention: Deposit an ultra-thin (nanometer-scale), dense ceramic coating of Al2O3 via physical vapor deposition (PVD) onto the existing boride surface.
generation.conditions: The components are exposed to high-temperature molten aluminum (700–750°C) under prolonged operational cycles typical of industrial hot-dip aluminum plating processes.
generation.structural_mediator: The continuous, dense Al2O3 barrier acts as an inert, thermally stable interface that blocks aluminum atoms from diffusing into the boride substrate.
generation.mechanism: By presenting a diffusion barrier, the ultra-thin ceramic coating inhibits the chemical interactions at the interface; this reduction in aluminum penetration slows or prevents interfacial degradation and subsequent corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coated components are expected to show a marked reduction in corrosion depth, lower aluminum diffusion at the interface, and reduced weight loss compared to untreated boride components when exposed to molten aluminum under the specified conditions.
generation.baseline: Untreated boride-based components that, upon exposure to molten aluminum at high temperatures, exhibit significant interfacial corrosion and measurable material degradation.
generation.boundary: The predicted improvement is expected under conditions replicating typical hot-dip plating cycles (700–750°C, prolonged exposure). However, the effectiveness may be sensitive to variables such as coating thickness, deposition uniformity, and extreme thermal cycling beyond standard operating conditions.
generation.uncertainty: While the mechanism is supported by trends in surface modification studies, the exact quantitative improvement in corrosion resistance remains uncertain due to potential variability in coating adhesion and thermal stress effects.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical boride-based components. Use PVD to deposit an ultra-thin Al2O3 coating on one set while leaving the other set uncoated as the control. Expose both sets to molten aluminum at 700–750°C under simulated industrial hot-dip plating conditions with repeated thermal cycles for a predetermined duration.
measurements: Cross-sectional scanning electron microscopy (SEM) to assess corrosion depth and interface integrity.
Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) or secondary ion mass spectrometry (SIMS) to quantify aluminum diffusion profiles.
Weight loss measurements to evaluate overall material degradation.
X-ray diffraction (XRD) to verify the stability of the Al2O3 coating and detect any phase changes.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples do not exhibit statistically significant reductions (p < 0.05) in corrosion depth, aluminum diffusion, or weight loss compared to uncoated controls—or if the coating fails (e.g., delaminates) under test conditions—the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this study, a reinforced layer was prepared on the surface of HEA by powder-pack boriding and focused on the effect of temperature and duration on the boronizing of CoCrFeNiMn HEA. The boronized samples were characterized using various methods. Furthermore, the properties of boronized CoCrFeNiMn alloys and diffusion behavior were investigated. This study could provide a reference for high hardness and high wear resistance HEA that could be used in a variety of industrial applications, such as the mold and crucible used in the cast aluminum industry [,], because the borides formed on the surface have high hardness, excellent corrosion resistance, and wear resistance [,], which allow HEA to be applied in special environments to increase service life.

In addition, to obtain a uniform and stable protective layer, sputtering technology offers a fast deposition rate and a low-cost solution. Although the development of HEA systems has been going on for more than a decade, there are few reports on the deposition of stable protective films on HEA surfaces by conventional reactive sputtering techniques. Many studies have shown that sputter deposition of CrN film on conventional stainless steel is beneficial for its wear and corrosion resistance [,]. The CrN film deposited on the surface of 316 stainless steel has a positive effect on the friction behavior in NaCl solution and high temperature environments until heated to 550 °C []. In the tribo-corrosion test, the CrN coating layer can also remain relatively stable during the ball-on-plate sliding under various applied potentials []. As stainless steels are similar to CoCrNi-based MEAs in terms of their single FCC structure and lattice constant, this study attempts to sputter CrN film with a Cr buffer layer on the surface of CoCrNiSi0.3 MEA and discusses in detail the improvement of corrosion and wear resistance of CoCrNiSi0.3 MEA by sputtering CrN film.

frame.system: Boride-based components used in hot‐dip aluminum‐plating equipment, which in their current state are directly exposed to molten aluminum at high temperatures.
frame.goal: Improve resistance of the components to corrosion by molten aluminum through a single, surface‐modification intervention.
frame.limitation: The current boride-based surfaces are vulnerable to attack by molten aluminum, likely because they lack an effective diffusion barrier or inert interphase to halt interfacial degradation.
constraints: The intervention must be a single, discrete modification (e.g., a surface treatment or coating) without altering the bulk composition of the component.
It must remain effective under high-temperature, prolonged exposure to molten aluminum typical of plating conditions.
frame.regime: Exposure to molten aluminum at plating temperatures (on the order of 700–750°C) over extended operational cycles, representative of industrial hot-dip conditions.
prior_attempts: Previous efforts (implied by the need for improvement) may have involved alloying adjustments or bulk composition changes that did not provide a sufficient barrier effect, or multiple interventions that are not easily implemented as a single solution.

decision.trend: Early studies in high‐temperature corrosion and surface modification first tackled corrosion issues by altering bulk alloy compositions and microstructures (as seen in HEA corrosion in molten salt and water environments), with later research shifting focus toward tailored surface treatments. For example, powder‐pack boriding (PMC10221107) was used to generate dense, hard boride layers as diffusion barriers for improved mechanical and wear resistance, and investigations into interface phenomena during aluminum contamination (PMC11382193) highlighted the importance of an inert interphase. Thus, the evolution has moved from bulk composition tuning to engineering the near-surface region to inhibit diffusion and interfacial degradation.
decision.unsolved: Despite these advances, the specific challenge of protecting boride‐based components from molten‐aluminum attack under prolonged high‐temperature plating conditions remains unsolved. No single, discrete surface modification has yet proven to create a stable, effective diffusion barrier that can prevent interfacial degradation without altering the bulk composition.
decision.lever: application of an ultra-thin, ceramic-based diffusion barrier coating (such as a PVD-deposited Al2O3 or TiN layer) on the existing boride surface
decision.why: This lever follows naturally from the trend where researchers are moving towards surface treatments that create stable interfacial layers. Ceramic coatings are known for their chemical inertness and high-temperature stability, and prior work on boriding demonstrates that controlling diffusion at the surface is effective. A thin ceramic layer would serve as an inert barrier to molten aluminum, addressing the root-cause cue by impeding aluminum diffusion into the boride, thereby improving corrosion resistance relative to untreated surfaces in hot-dip conditions.
